'''''Lomatia fraseri''''', commonly known as '''tree lomatia''', '''forest lomatia''' or '''silky lomatia''' is a plant of the family [[Proteaceae]] native to eastern Australia. It grows as a shrub or small tree, reaching {{convert|8|–|11|m}} high, with highly variable leaves. The cream to white [[inflorescence]]s appear over summer. It is found in [[rainforest]] margins, gullies and heathland in mountainous regions of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[New South Wales]]. It regenerates from fire by regrowing from a [[lignotuber]].

==Description==
''Lomatia fraseri'' grows as a tall shrub or small tree up to 8–11 metres (25–36 ft) high,<ref name=FOA/> though can be much smaller in exposed areas; on heathland in [[Werrikimbe National Park]] it is reduced to a height of 50 cm (20 in), and can be {{cvt|2|m}} high in exposed areas in Victoria.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991">{{cite book|last=Wrigley |first=John |last2=Fagg |first2=Murray |title=Banksias, Waratahs and Grevilleas |year=1991 |publisher=Angus & Robertson |location=Sydney |isbn=0-207-17277-3 |pages=449–50}}</ref> It has lanceolate to elliptic leaves which range from entire to deeply pinnatisect and are between 6.5 and 15 (rarely 18) cm long and 1 to 3.5 (rarely 5) cm wide. The leaf margins are generally toothed, though occasionally entire or deeply lobed.<ref name=FOA/> The leaves are highly variable, and can even be markedly different on the same plant.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/> The upper surfaces are green and glabrous, while the undersides are yellow-green and silky.<ref name=NSW/> The individual flowers are arranged in [[raceme]]s that are up to 12 cm (5 in) long.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/> They can be more crowded than those of other lomatias.<ref name=EJ93>{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake. Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation |volume=6 – K-M|year=1993 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-589-9|page=231}}</ref> These white to cream [[inflorescence]]s appear between December and February in the species' native range, followed by the development of {{Convert|1.5 to 3|cm|4=1|abbr=on}} long dark grey follicles, which are ripe from April to October.<ref name=FOA/><ref name=NSW/>

==Taxonomy==
Scottish botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] described ''Lomatia fraseri'' in his 1830 work ''[[Supplementum primum Prodromi florae Novae Hollandiae]]'', from a specimen that had been collected in the Sydney district (then known as Port Jackson) by [[Charles Fraser (botanist)|Charles Fraser]] in 1818.<ref name=FOA/> George Bentham lumped ''L. fraseri'' and ''L ilicifolia'' together, treating them as one species in his 1870 work ''[[Flora Australiensis]]''.<ref name="Bentham 1870">{{cite encyclopedia |author=Bentham, George |year=1870 |title=''Lomatia ilicfolia'' |encyclopedia=[[Wikisource:Flora Australiensis|Flora Australiensis]] |volume=5: Myoporineae to Proteaceae |pages=536–37|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11622350 |location=London, UK|publisher=L. Reeve & Co. |author-link=George Bentham}}</ref>

Hybrids have been recorded with the river lomatia (''[[Lomatia myricoides]]'') on the Southern Tablelands, resulting in plants resembling ''L. fraseri'' but less hairy, and with crinkle bush (''L. silaifolia'') in the [[New England (Australia)|New England]] area, resulting in plants with highly variable leaf shapes and hairy leaf undersides. Hybrids with native holly (''[[Lomatia ilicifolia|L. ilicifolia]]'') have been recorded, the resulting plants having variable hairiness and prickliness.<ref name=FOA/> Analysis of [[chloroplast]] DNA showed that there is extensive hybridization between the five species (''L. arborescens'', ''L. fraseri'', ''L. ilicifolia'', ''L. myricoides'' and ''L. silaifolia'') of mainland southeastern Australia, though each is distinct enough to warrant species status.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Milner|first=Melita|author2=Rossetto, Maurizio |author3=Crisp, Michael D. |author4=Weston, Peter H. |date=2012|title=The impact of multiple biogeographic barriers and hybridization on species-level differentiation|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=99|issue=12|pages=2045–57 | doi=10.3732/ajb.1200327 |pmid=23221499}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Lomatia fraseri'' has a disjunct distribution, being found in the New England district of northern New South Wales north to Tenterfield and from [[Budawang National Park]] in southern New South Wales into eastern and central [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] to the [[Otway Ranges]]. It is found in [[rainforest]] margins in mountainous regions.<ref name=FOA>{{Flora of Australia Online|name=''Lomatia fraseri''|id=45143}}</ref><ref name=NSW>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Lomatia~fraseri |title=''Lomatia fraseri'' |access-date=2009-04-27 |last=Harden |first=G. J. |work=PlantNET – New South Wales Flora Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney Australia}}</ref> Often found in gullies in Victoria, it grows more in open woodland and heath in New South Wales.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/>

''Lomatia frasieri'' has been documented as being naturalised in New Zealand.<ref>{{CiteQ|Q118223183}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Lomatia fraseri'' regenerates after bushfire by resprouting from a [[lignotuber]]. Fieldwork in the Central Highlands of Victoria predicts populations will be adversely affected by clearfelling and salvage logging after bushfires there.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Lindenmayer|first=D.B.|author2=Ough, K. |date=2005|title=Salvage Logging in the Montane Ash Eucalypt Forests of the Central Highlands of Victoria and Its Potential Impacts on Biodiversity|journal=Conservation Biology|volume=20|issue=4|pages=1005–15 |doi=10.1111/j.1523-1739.2006.00501.x |pmid=16922217|url=http://www.sierraforestlegacy.org/Resources/Conservation/FireForestEcology/SalvageLoggingScience/Salvage-Lindenmayer06b.pdf}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
The marked variation in leaf shape are an interesting horticultural feature.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/> ''Lomatia fraseri'' grows in sun or preferably part-shade, benefiting from extra watering when young and from organic mulch. It is moderately frost-tolerant.<ref name=EJ93/> Propagation is by seed or cutting.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/>

[[Joseph Maiden]] reported that its wood was light and hard, and easily worked.<ref>{{cite book|last=Maiden|first=Joseph Henry|title=The useful native plants of Australia, (including Tasmania)|publisher=Turner and Henderson|location=Sydney, New South Wales|date=1889|pages=564|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/12453767}}</ref> It had been used for furniture and window-frames in the 19th century.<ref>{{cite book|author=Committee of the Royal Society of Victoria|title=Transactions of the Philosophical Institute of Victoria from January to December|publisher=Government Printing Office|location=Melbourne, Victoria|date=1859|volume=III|pages=24|chapter=Indigenous Vegetable Productions|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EsY1AQAAIAAJ&q=%22Lomatia+fraseri%22&pg=RA3-PA24}}</ref>
